France’s government faces a deepening political test after nationwide protests over living costs and public services descended into the country’s worst unrest in years. Around 550,000 people marched on Saturday, with almost 2,400 arrested and nearly 1,000 police officers injured. Rioters attacked public buildings and shops. At the same time many demonstrators protested peacefully but found their peaceful protests hijacked by rioters and looters. ... US President Donald Trump has endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of the October 27 election, praising his leadership during the joint US-Israeli war against Iran. Trump also suggested further American action against Iran could depend on Netanyahu remaining in office, saying he was reluctant to act alone under another Israeli leader. ... Saudi Arabia’s advanced military is struggling to contain Houthi missile and drone attacks, exposing weaknesses in its air defences despite one of the world’s largest defence budgets. A strike on Riyadh’s international airport killed at least 13 people, while another attack injured six in Najran on Sunday. Saudi officials face shortages of missile interceptors and the challenge of protecting infrastructure spread across vast territory. ... Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has refused to resign after six days of student-led protests, warning that the unrest threatens the country’s ambition to join the European Union. Demonstrations over alleged corruption, unemployment and poor education standards have spread from Tirana to other cities. Protesters have attacked government buildings, banks and shops, while police have used tear gas, water cannon and rubber bullets. ... The United States has resumed intelligence sharing on Russian ballistic missile launches after a three day interruption, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sunday. Ukraine relies on American warnings to detect incoming missiles but alerts came only after five Russian missiles struck Kyiv on October 12. Zelensky said the service was now restored, although restrictions on Ukraine’s Starshield satellite communications remain in place. ... NATO fighter jets scrambled over Lithuania on Sunday after a suspected drone entered its airspace and apparently exploded, forcing residents in northern and central areas to shelter for an hour. Kaunas airport temporarily closed and debris struck a civilian vehicle. Two Italian Eurofighters responded but could not identify the object through cloud cover. ... Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a summit with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to discuss ending the Ukraine war without Ukrainian participation. The meeting could take place alongside November’s APEC summit in Shenzhen. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed discussions but said neither the meeting nor its agenda had been agreed. ... The format would exclude Ukraine and European governments from discussions about the war’s settlement. China has indicated it would not object if Trump agreed, although he has not committed. The prospect has alarmed Kyiv and European allies concerned about a settlement favouring Moscow. Kenya has confirmed an eighth Ebola infection as an outbreak originating in the Democratic Republic of Congo continues to spread across East Africa. Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth said one of 38 people tested on Sunday was positive. The 49-year-old patient attendant, who cleaned utensils and linens, was probably exposed to Kenya’s first case, a traveller from Congo who died in Nairobi on October 5. ... Congo has recorded at least 9,400 cases and more than 4,500 deaths since May. The virus has now reached eight Congolese provinces, while North Kivu authorities plan restrictions on arrivals from neighbouring Ituri. Uganda previously recorded 20 cases and two deaths before being declared Ebola-free in August.

items.title: Treasury yields move lower as investors assess U.S. inflation backdrop
items.excerpt: Treasury yields moved higher on Monday as investors continue to weigh the domestic inflation and interest rate backdrop against broader geopolitical developments. The yield on 10-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — rose more than 3 basis points to 5.136%. The longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury Add To Watchlist bond yield — which often moves on geopolitical developments — was also more than 3 basis points higher at 5.471%. The yield on the 2-year Treasury note Add To Watchlist, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, was up more than 3 basis points at 4.772%. ... The moves come as inflation concerns continue to loom over the U.S. economy. Last week's strong inflation data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics saw wholesale prices rise 6.3% annually last month — the biggest jump since 2022 — with consumer costs up 3.7% annually in September, beating estimates. Meanwhile, energy prices fell Monday as investors continued to weigh the possibility of more Russian crude supply coming onto the market. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures Add To Watchlist for November delivery were down 0.3% at $101.11 per barrel. Brent crude Add To Watchlist, the global oil price benchmark, dropped 1.2% to $108.56. With the Federal Reserve's next interest rate decision due Oct. 28, traders are now pricing in an above-80% probability that the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will leave borrowing costs unchanged, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

items.title: Hassett says inflation "needing some work" By Investing.com
items.excerpt: Investing.com -- White House National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said Monday that inflation requires policy attention after September consumer price data showed continued pressure, though prices have declined for some items including beef and eggs. "If you look at the previous three months, it looked like inflation was completely under control, and now it looks like it's sort of back needing some work," Hassett told CNBC Monday. Consumer price data released last week showed prices rose in September at the fastest pace in five months. The consumer price index increased 0.6% from the previous month. A measure of underlying price pressures that excludes food and energy rose 0.3%, exceeding expectations. "This is either a sort of break from the downtrend or a blip," Hassett said in the interview. Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh last week did not address market expectations that the central bank will keep interest rates unchanged at its meeting later this month. During a moderated discussion at the International Monetary Fund's annual meetings, Warsh made no comments on monetary policy or his economic outlook beyond stating the Fed will deliver price stability. Hassett said he respects the central bank's independence and noted Warsh will "do what he thinks is the right thing." ... "People are really euphoric about how well the economy is doing, and they're spending more. And of course, that's the kind of thing the Fed needs to pay attention to," Hassett said.

items.title: United States: October inflation seen cooling – TD Securities
items.excerpt: TD Securities economists Oscar Munoz and Eli Nir project that US headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) will rise 0.30% month-on-month in October 2026, slowing from September’s 0.65% gain, with gasoline and food still contributing. They expect core CPI to increase 0.21% and translate into a 0.24% rise in core Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index, as core goods and services inflation moderate and shelter cools. ## TD sees softer but still solid CPI ... "Following the release of the September CPI report, we are providing an early look into our October projection based on multiple assumptions which may evolve as the month progresses and more data becomes available — particularly for volatile segments like gasoline prices, hotel rates, and airfares." ... "Headline inflation is expected to cool down in October, rising a still solid 0.30% m/m after a stronger 0.65% m/m September increase (CPI NSA index: 337.316 vs the market's current fixing at 337.250)." "Our preliminary forecast for the October core CPI stands at 0.21% m/m (down from a firmer 0.33% gain in September), which would be consistent with a core PCE increase at 0.24%." "Core goods prices likely lost some momentum on the back of a decline in used vehicle prices and cooling from apparel, recreation and IT goods. A pickup in household goods prices likely acted as a partial offset to the broad decline." ... "Services inflation is projected to mean-revert following last month's broad-based increase. We look for shelter to throttle down — led by a reversal in OER — after an unexpected surge in the last report. Slowing inflation in transportation and recreation services is also expected to help tame price gains in the segment."

items.title: Emma Freud says Beatles' songs to star in Yesterday musical
items.excerpt: Emma Freud says Beatles' songs to star in Yesterday musical # Freud confirms Beatles' songs to star in musical 18 minutes ago Mariam Issimdar Jeff Spicer/Getty Images Screenwriter Richard Curtis and his wife Emma Freud are looking to bring the movie Yesterday on to the theatre stage Film producer Emma Freud has confirmed The Beatles have agreed for their songs to feature in a stage version of the movie, Yesterday. Freud is working on the show with her husband, Richard Curtis. They were behind the 2019 film and other box office hits, including Love Actually and Bridget Jones's Diary. She called it "a huge deal", saying: "They've [The Beatles] never done that with a West End musical before. So it's the first time that you can kind of legally see The Beatles' music on stage, which is amazing." Freud spoke to BBC Radio Suffolk on Monday, after she received an honorary doctorate for her work in film and broadcasting at the University of Suffolk on Saturday. University of Suffolk Emma Freud received an honorary doctorate in Ipswich on Saturday She said a theatre where the stage show will be performed had been chosen - "but I can't tell you what it is because I will get killed". She confirmed the stage version of Yesterday would also be directed by Oscar-winner Danny Boyle, who oversaw the movie. Freud said: "We're at workshop stages, so we've already had two workshops and we've got a third one coming up this month, where you sort of ask actors to come into a room and just interrogate the script and the songs and the staging, and see how it's going to work. "Currently we're on the 11th draft of the script, because it isn't just taking a movie script and putting it on to a stage. "It's the same story, but actually every beat of it becomes different, becomes theatrical rather than filmic. "So it's been an incredible process to be a part of. I don't feel like I've ever done anything as big in my entire life." The Beatles were one of the biggest bands on the planet, with a multitude of hits including Hey Jude, Let it Be and Yesterday Yesterday is about a struggling musician who wakes up one day to find an altered world where no-one has heard of The Beatles. He becomes famous after singing their songs and passing them off as his own. The film stars Himesh Patel and Lily James, along with Suffolk-based singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran. It was shot throughout Suffolk, Essex and Norfolk, including a scene with 6,000 extras in Gorleston-on-Sea. Richard Curtis with the lead actor in the film Yesterday, Himesh Patel On receiving her doctorate from the University of Suffolk, Freud said "the honour" was "so massive", because "Suffolk is my home and it's where I was brought up, and it's where my family has lived for generations". Her family arrived in the county as Jewish refugees from Germany in the 1930s, escaping the tyranny of the Nazis. Freud's work has also involved tackling poverty and inequality, and has included working as a creative director and executive producer at Comic Relief. University of Suffolk
